content.title: The Mole Concept — Study Book
content.introduction: Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in batches called moles. This book shows how the mole links a number of particles to a mass you can weigh on a balance.

diagnostic.prompt: A water molecule is H₂O. How many hydrogen atoms does one molecule contain?

subtopics.title: The mole and the Avogadro constant
subtopics.key_idea: One mole of any substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Number of particles = moles × Avogadro constant.
explanation: The mole is the chemist's counting unit, like a dozen but far larger. One mole contains exactly 6.022 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant.
The particles can be atoms, molecules or ions, so always say which particle you are counting. One mole of water molecules contains three moles of atoms.
To convert, multiply moles by 6.022 × 10²³ to get particles, or divide particles by 6.022 × 10²³ to get moles.
subtopics.misconception: A mole is not a mass; it is an amount (a count). Its mass depends on which substance you have.

worked_example.problem: How many atoms are in 2 mol of helium atoms?
steps: Write the relationship: number of particles = moles × Avogadro constant.
Calculate and state the particle: 1.2044 × 10²⁴ helium atoms.

visual.title: Particles grow in step with moles
visual.desc: Bars showing 6.022, 12.044 and 18.066 (×10²³ particles) for 1, 2 and 3 mol.

reconstruct.prompt: Explain in your own words why chemists count particles in moles rather than one by one.
reconstruct.model_answer: Particles are so small that even a drop of water contains about 10²¹ molecules. Grouping them in moles of 6.022 × 10²³ turns impossible counts into small numbers that link directly to weighable masses.

subtopics.syllabus: Molar mass and conversion between mass and amount of substance
subtopics.title: Molar mass and mass–mole conversion
subtopics.key_idea: Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in g/mol, found by adding atomic masses. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
explanation: Add the atomic masses of every atom in the formula to get the molar mass. For water, H₂O: 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 g/mol.
To find the amount of substance, divide the mass in grams by the molar mass. To find the mass, multiply the moles by the molar mass.
Keep units visible: g ÷ (g/mol) = mol, and mol × (g/mol) = g. The units check the direction of the calculation.
subtopics.misconception: Forgetting the subscript: the molar mass of H₂O counts two hydrogen atoms, not one.

worked_example.problem: How many moles are in 88 g of carbon dioxide? (C = 12, O = 16)
steps: Moles = 2 mol; check the units: g ÷ (g/mol) = mol.

visual.title: Molar masses of common substances
visual.desc: Bars for water 18, carbon dioxide 44 and sodium chloride 58.5 g/mol.

reconstruct.prompt: Explain how you would decide whether 10 g of water or 10 g of carbon dioxide contains more molecules.
reconstruct.model_answer: Convert each mass to moles by dividing by the molar mass: 10 ÷ 18 for water and 10 ÷ 44 for carbon dioxide. Water has the smaller molar mass, so it has more moles and therefore more molecules.

subtopics.title: Percentage composition
subtopics.key_idea: The percentage of an element in a compound is its total mass in one mole divided by the molar mass, times 100.
explanation: Find the molar mass of the compound, then the mass contributed by the element in one mole, counting every atom of that element in the formula.
Divide that contribution by the molar mass and multiply by 100 to get the percentage by mass.
The percentages of all the elements in a compound add up to 100, which is a useful check.
subtopics.misconception: Using the number of atoms instead of their mass: water has two hydrogen atoms but hydrogen is only about 11% of its mass.

worked_example.problem: Find the percentage of carbon by mass in carbon dioxide. (C = 12, O = 16)
steps: Mass of carbon in one mole = 12 g.
Percentage of carbon = 12 ÷ 44 × 100 ≈ 27.3%; oxygen is therefore about 72.7%.

visual.title: Mass composition of carbon dioxide
visual.desc: Bars for carbon 27.3% and oxygen 72.7% by mass.

reconstruct.prompt: Explain why the percentage of hydrogen in water is small even though water has twice as many hydrogen atoms as oxygen atoms.
reconstruct.model_answer: Percentage composition is by mass. Each hydrogen atom has mass 1 and the oxygen atom has mass 16, so the two hydrogens contribute only 2 of the 18 g in a mole, about 11%.
